S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Incidents involving fire, injury, evacuation, or property damage must be reported within 24 hours of discovery; other thermal incidents must be reported within five business days. Affected customers must be notified within 48 hours for urgent incidents and within five business days for other reportable incidents.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator. Incidents involving fire, injury, evacuation, or property damage must be reported within 24 hours of discovery; other thermal incidents must be reported within five business days. Affected customers must be notified within 48 hours for urgent incidents and within five business days for other reportable incidents. Reports must include known safety risks and relevant model and lot identification.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: A failure rate above 5% requires a regulator-reviewed corrective-action plan and retesting; it does not by itself prohibit sale or require withdrawal. Customers who buy a model must receive its per-model test results and any relevant safety information in an accessible form; this does not require general-public publication of individual-company results.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol. Manufacturers must submit complete per-model results to the relevant regulator and retain them for audit. Customers who buy a model must receive its per-model test results and any relevant safety information in an accessible form; this does not require general-public publication of individual-company results. A failure rate above 5% requires a regulator-reviewed corrective-action plan and retesting; it does not by itself prohibit sale or require withdrawal. Regulators may impose additional measures based on the results and demonstrated risk.

parameters.quote: All new home battery units must include a remote emergency shut-off capability no later than 12 months after adoption. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that lack this capability within six years after adoption, where technically feasible... Any unit that cannot be safely retrofitted must be identified to its owner and the relevant regulator, with an alternative safe decommissioning or replacement plan.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: All new home battery units must include a remote emergency shut-off capability no later than 12 months after adoption. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that lack this capability within six years after adoption, where technically feasible... Any unit that cannot be safely retrofitted must be identified to its owner and the relevant regulator, with an alternative safe decommissioning or replacement plan.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new home battery units must include a remote emergency shut-off capability no later than 12 months after adoption. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that lack this capability within six years after adoption, where technically feasible, and must notify affected customers of the capability and how to use it. Any unit that cannot be safely retrofitted must be identified to its owner and the relevant regulator, with an alternative safe decommissioning or replacement plan.

parameters.quote: All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The suppression system must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and designed to reduce the risk of fire spread and harm to occupants and neighbours.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The suppression system must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and designed to reduce the risk of fire spread and harm to occupants and neighbours.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The suppression system must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and designed to reduce the risk of fire spread and harm to occupants and neighbours. Manufacturers must provide evidence of its effectiveness through regulator-approved testing.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the relevant regulator and provide the underlying incident-rate data and a corrective-action plan. A recall is mandatory when the regulator determines that a continuing unacceptable thermal risk cannot be adequately controlled by other measures.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Customers must receive clear safety notices promptly when a product presents a credible thermal hazard, including the affected model or lot, the nature of the risk, and steps to reduce exposure or obtain assistance. When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the relevant regulator and provide the underlying incident-rate data and a corrective-action plan. The regulator must review the evidence and determine whether a recall is required, taking account of the severity and circumstances of incidents, data quality, and the effectiveness of corrective actions. A recall is mandatory when the regulator determines that a continuing unacceptable thermal risk cannot be adequately controlled by other measures. The manufacturer must notify affected customers without delay and provide a remedy plan whenever a recall is required.

We support regulator access to per-model results and meaningful customer safety notices, but oppose public disclosure of individual-company per-model failure rates. A fixed 5% market-eligibility ceiling would exclude products without accounting for remediation or protocol differences.

judge_section_notes: The final S2 keeps the 5% failure benchmark but removes any sales stop, so a model above it can keep being sold under a corrective-action plan, which protects Northwind's Hearth 10. S5 replaces the 8-per-100k recall trigger with regulator discretion and an open corrective-action alternative, so no numeric recall is mandatory, which protects Halcyon's Ember 8. S3 (six-year retrofit) and S4 (36-month suppression) sit at the edges of the acceptable ranges, favouring Northwind and Halcyon respectively.
